tagline.text: Twin falls whose mist rises beneath a cliffside staircase in the hills of Kabankalan

location.label: Location
location.text: Sitio Dug-anon, Barangay Oringao, Kabankalan City, Negros Occidental (Mag-aso Leisure Camp)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,500 (day round trip from Bacolod, including transport, entrance and lunch)

children.text: Mag-aso Falls is a set of twin falls in the hills of Kabankalan City, Negros Occidental, and its mist rises like smoke, hence the name, since aso means smoke. From the city-run leisure camp you go down a cliffside staircase to the falls and a swimming pool.

Mag-aso Falls lies in the hills of Barangay Oringao in Kabankalan City, in the southwest of Negros Island. Aso is the Hiligaynon word for smoke, and the name is said to come from the mist the falls throw up, which looks like smoke. The falls are described as twin falls, and sources differ widely on their height, from around 8 m to 23 m, so this guide does not commit to a single figure.

The entrance to the falls is the city-run Mag-aso Leisure Camp. The camp has a swimming pool, cottages, shed houses, a canteen and store, a camping area, rooms and a multipurpose hall that seats 70. The falls are below the cliff under the camp, and you have to go down roughly 100 steps of a concrete and steel staircase with railings. This staircase is the signature feature of the place and its hardest stretch. The climb back up is especially tiring.

This is not a place to go straight to from Manila. It is a day trip you fit in along the western coastal road of Negros, between Bacolod and Sipalay. It is a different place from the waterfall of the same name in Bohol, so check on your map app that you have the Kabankalan one. Local reports say the Kabankalan site was closed for more than a year and then reopened with renovated facilities in December 2021.

Visitors praise the quiet mountain atmosphere away from the city, the cool water in front of the falls and the convenience of the swimming pool. On the other hand, be aware that transport is scarce, the stairs are tiring in both directions, and the river turns muddy after rain. If you go by public transport, it is especially important to arrange your return ride in advance. When planning, keep in mind that the travel time is much longer than the time you spend at the falls. From Bacolod, the round trip takes up most of a day, so rather than making the falls your destination, it is more efficient to stop by on the way south to Sipalay or Dumaguete. Kabankalan sits in the middle of Negros sugarcane country, and from the window you can see endless cane fields and mountain scenery.

blocks.title: Twin falls that rise like smoke

children.text: Mist spreads like fog below the falls, so you can see for yourself where the name comes from. In the morning or on cloudy days, the mist can look even more distinct.

A staircase with railings and rest landings runs from the camp to the falls. Reviews give slightly different step counts, and you will need to pace your water and energy on the way up. Some reviews say older visitors can make it by going slowly, since there are places to rest along the way, but do not push yourself if your knees are bad.

blocks.title: A large pool fed by the falls

children.text: The camp has a large swimming pool fed by water from the falls, and some are said to be split into children's and adults' areas. It is shallower and safer than the river, so it suits visits with children.
There is a viewing area in front of the falls, and you can dip your feet in the river that flows below. The current is strong, so if you are not a confident swimmer, play only in the shallows.
The most common way to enjoy the visit is to rent a cottage by the pool and eat a packed lunch. Cottage rates depend on size, and on weekends they fill up early, so arrive early.
There are a camping area and rooms, so some visitors stay overnight and see the falls in the morning. Check current rates.
Reviews say the mountain road from the Oringao junction to the camp entrance, past white cliffs and rivers, is a sight in itself.

items.title: Day trip from Bacolod
items.subtitle: Morning bus to Kabankalan, falls in the afternoon

children.text: Take a bus to Kabankalan from the Bacolod South Terminal. The ride is reported to take about
2–3 hours
In Kabankalan, take a tricycle toward the market, then a jeepney toward Mabinay, and get off at the Mag-aso junction in Oringao.
From the junction, take a tricycle or motorcycle taxi (habal-habal) up to the leisure camp. Agree on a pickup time for the return with your driver.

Pay the entrance fee at the camp, walk down the stairs and enjoy the falls. Have lunch at the pool and cottages. Catch your breath at the rest stops along the stairs and go down slowly. At the viewing area in front of the falls, take photos away from the spot where the most spray lands.
Climb back up, tidy up and ride down to the junction at the time you arranged. Move on to Bacolod or your next stop before dark.
Public transport runs infrequently and thins out later in the day, so start early. Hiring a vehicle makes it much easier.

items.title: Overnight at the camp
items.subtitle: A relaxed plan that includes the morning mist

children.text: Arrive at the camp, settle into your room and relax at the pool.
Eat nearby or eat the food you brought. The store menu is limited.
Go down the stairs to the falls when few people are around, enjoy the mist and the sunlight, and leave before lunch.
Rates for rooms and camping differ from review to review, so confirm them locally.

items.title: By air from Manila to Bacolod

children.text: There are direct flights from Manila (NAIA) to Bacolod–Silay International Airport (BCD). The flight takes about
1 hour 20 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes
From the airport, go into Bacolod by taxi or airport van. Check flight schedules and fares on the airline's website.

items.title: By bus from Bacolod to Kabankalan

children.text: Take a bus toward Kabankalan or Dumaguete from the Bacolod South Terminal. The ride takes about
2–3 hours
Kabankalan is about
88km
from Bacolod. It can take longer depending on traffic.
Bus schedules and fares change often, so confirm them at the ticket counter.
From town, take a tricycle toward the public market, then a jeepney toward Mabinay and get off at the Mag-aso junction in Oringao.
From the junction to the leisure camp at the falls entrance, use a tricycle or habal-habal. The camp is described as about
18km
from the city hall area, and some reviews say it takes about
20–30 minutes
by car.
Few tricycles wait in front of the camp. Arrange your ride back in advance.

In the November–May dry season, the roads are dry and the river is clear, which is good for swimming and photos. When it rains, the river can turn brown, which is a sign of rain upstream, so do not enter the river.
On weekends, local families flood in and the cottages fill up early. Weekday mornings are the quietest and easiest.

During peak times such as Holy Week, the year-end holidays and the May school break, local groups increase and the stairs and pool get crowded. If you go then, arrive early to secure a cottage, rest at the pool in the middle of the day, and visit the falls again in the afternoon to avoid the crowds.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: The water is clear and walking is pleasant, so this is the most recommended time.
Good for swimming, but the sun is strong on the mountain road.
The stairs are slippery and the river can rise, so take care.

The camp has rooms and a camping area, but it is small and has no published rate card, so confirm on site. Kabankalan town has ordinary hotels and guesthouses, so if you stay more than one night, it is steadier to use the town as a base and hire a vehicle for the trip.

The camp store is said to sell little more than drinks, snacks and simple local food, so it is safer to buy lunch in town or pack a meal. In town you can easily find Negros-style grilled dishes, chicken dishes and Bacolod snacks. Names of nearby places change often, so check recent reviews on a map app.

Renting a private car or a car with a driver is the most comfortable way. Hiring one for a day from Bacolod lets you see the falls and nearby small towns together, and since you only walk the staircase section, it is also less of a burden with children or older travelers. Fares vary widely with distance and bargaining, so agree on the price before you leave, including waiting time for the round trip. In the rainy season the mountain road can be slippery or flooded, so ask your driver about current road conditions.
Start early in the morning if you plan to take buses and jeepneys. Vehicles become scarce late in the afternoon.
Arrange your return tricycle in advance and fix a time.
Non-slip sandals or sneakers are best on the stairs. Going barefoot or in flip-flops is dangerous.
Bring a waterproof bag, a change of clothes and a towel. There is a lot of spray in front of the falls.
Bring plenty of water and snacks, and carry cash in small bills. Cards are hard to use.
If you have children, use the camp pool rather than the falls, and have an adult stay beside them.
To avoid confusion with the waterfall of the same name in Bohol, check that your map shows Kabankalan.
Cottages fill up early on weekends, so we recommend a weekday morning visit.
Wear a light cover-up over your swimwear so it is easier on the stairs.
Keep your camera in a waterproof pouch. Spray beads on the lens in front of the falls.
If the river is brown after rain, it means rain fell upstream, so do not enter the river. It is not confirmed whether lifeguards are present, so swim with care.
The stairs are steep and slippery when wet. Hold the railing as you move.
The small pool below the falls has a strong current, so enter only if you are a confident swimmer.
Transport is scarce, so plan to be back at your lodging before dark.
Hours and entrance fees may change because this is a city-run facility. Check current information with the Kabankalan City tourism office or the camp.
Mobile signal can be weak on the mountain road. Save an offline map.
The camp facilities are city-managed, so there may be visitor limits or temporary closures at peak times and on holidays. Contact them before you leave to confirm.

A university city in Negros Oriental to the south, connected overland from Kabankalan. It is a long trip, so allow plenty of time.
